extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers working on partial differential equations and Sobolev-space methods
extracted.subtask_description: Mathematical statements, hypotheses, and techniques for existence, uniqueness, regularity, maximum principle, and energy estimates for the heat (parabolic) and wave (hyperbolic) equations in Sobolev-space frameworks. Includes both abstract semigroup/variational criteria and concrete conditions on data, coefficients, and domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat equation existence and uniqueness (Theorem 10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume u0 ∈ L2(Ω). Then there exists a unique function u(x,t) satisfying ∂u/∂t − Δu = 0 in Q, u = 0 on lateral boundary, u(x,0)=u0, and u ∈ C([0,∞);L2(Ω)) ∩ C((0,∞); H2(Ω) ∩ H1 0 (Ω)), u ∈ C1((0,∞);L2(Ω)), u ∈ L2(0,∞;H1 0 (Ω)), and u ∈ C∞(Ω × [ε,∞)) for every ε>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses include a smooth bounded domain (assumed throughout chapter for simplicity) and incorporation of the Dirichlet boundary condition into the operator domain. Proof uses Hille–Yosida theory by defining A with D(A)=H2∩H1 0 and Au=−Δu and checking A is self-adjoint maximal monotone. Energy identity (6) holds: (1/2)|u(T)|2_L2 + ∫_0^T |∇u(t)|2_L2 dt = (1/2)|u0|2_L2. Method remarks: other choices of H (e.g., H1_0) possible; separation-of-variables (eigenfunction expansion) also available when Ω bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporating boundary conditions into operator domain
rubrics_metrics.description: When setting up the unbounded operator A for semigroup methods, the boundary condition (e.g., Dirichlet u=0) is enforced by defining the domain D(A) to consist of functions satisfying the boundary condition (e.g., D(A)=H2(Ω) ∩ H1 0 (Ω)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is used repeatedly (heat and wave problems). It ensures the semigroup generator reflects the PDE boundary conditions and simplifies functional-analytic proofs of well-posedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat equation smoothing effect and time irreversibility (Remark 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The heat equation has a strong smoothing effect: for any t>0 the solution u(·,t) is C∞ in x even if initial data u0 is discontinuous. Consequently, the heat equation is time-irreversible and the backward problem (final data prescribed at t=T) may fail to have a solution unless extremely restrictive compatibility/smoothness conditions hold on the final data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: attempting to solve the backward heat problem from arbitrary L2 final data; even C∞ final data with vanishing boundary derivatives may not suffice. Use caution: smoothing forward does not imply solvability backward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity ladder for heat equation (Theorem 10.2(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If u0 ∈ H1 0 (Ω) then the solution u of the heat problem satisfies u ∈ C([0,∞); H1 0 (Ω)) ∩ L2(0,∞; H2(Ω)) and ∂u/∂t ∈ L2(0,∞; L2(Ω)), with the energy identity (7): ∫_0^T ||∂u/∂t(t)||2_L2 dt + (1/2)||∇u(T)||2_L2 = (1/2)||∇u0||2_L2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work in H1_0 as the base Hilbert space and apply Hille–Yosida to the appropriate operator A1 with domain D(A1)= {u ∈ H3∩H1_0; Δu ∈ H1_0}. Theorem shows gain of spatial regularity and control of time derivative in L2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity ladder for heat equation (Theorem 10.2(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work in H2 equipped with an equivalent scalar product and apply Hille–Yosida to operator A2 with D(A2)= {u ∈ H4; u ∈ H1 0, Δu ∈ H1 0}. Shows further regularity gain when initial data is smoother.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite smoothness via compatibility conditions (Theorem 10.2(c) and (8))
rubrics_metrics.description: If u0 ∈ Hk(Ω) for all k and satisfies the compatibility conditions u0 = Δu0 = ··· = Δ^j u0 = 0 on ∂Ω for every integer j, then the solution u is C∞ on Ω × [0,∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility conditions are necessary (and, with the stated hypotheses, sufficient) to obtain smoothness up to t=0. These conditions arise by equating time derivatives (evaluated at t=0) with spatial powers of Δ and enforcing boundary vanishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy identity for the heat equation (estimate (6))
rubrics_metrics.description: For the solution u of the homogeneous heat problem, (1/2)||u(T)||2_L2 + ∫_0^T ||∇u(t)||2_L2 dt = (1/2)||u0||2_L2 for all T>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by multiplying the PDE by u and integrating in space-time, with attention to regularity at t=0 (use truncation/limiting). This identity provides a priori control of L2 norms and gradient integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum principle for the heat equation (Theorem 10.3 and Corollaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u0 ∈ L2(Ω) and u is the solution of the heat problem, then for all (x,t) ∈ Ω×(0,∞), min(0, inf_Ω u0) ≤ u(x,t) ≤ max(0, sup_Ω u0). Consequences: positivity preservation (if u0 ≥ 0 a.e. then u ≥ 0), L∞ bound ||u||_L∞(Q) ≤ ||u0||_L∞(Ω), and continuity if u0 ∈ C(Ω)∩L2 with u0=0 on ∂Ω implies u ∈ C(Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Stampacchia truncation method and energy estimates; alternative approach uses parabolic boundary principle (Theorem 10.6). Useful a priori control and stability; use approximation by smooth compactly supported initial data to obtain continuity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic maximum principle (Theorem 10.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For u ∈ C(Ω×[0,T]) with C1 in t and C2 in x on Ω×(0,T) satisfying ∂u/∂t − Δu ≤ 0 in Ω×(0,T), the maximum of u over Ω×[0,T] is attained on the parabolic boundary P = (Ω×{0}) ∪ (∂Ω×[0,T]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard device: perturb u by ε|x|^2 to obtain strict inequality and exclude interior maxima. This yields the boundary localization of maxima for subsolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave equation existence, uniqueness, and energy conservation (Theorem 10.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume u0 ∈ H2(Ω) ∩ H1 0 (Ω) and v0 ∈ H1 0 (Ω). Then there exists a unique solution u of ∂^2_t u − Δu = 0 with u=0 on lateral boundary, u(·,0)=u0, ∂u/∂t(·,0)=v0, and u ∈ C([0,∞);H2∩H1 0 )∩C1([0,∞);H1 0 )∩C2([0,∞);L2). Moreover the energy is conserved: ||∂u/∂t(t)||2_L2 + ||∇u(t)||2_L2 = ||v0||2_L2 + ||∇u0||2_L2 for all t≥0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite as first-order system U' + A U = 0 (U=(u,v)), choose H = H1_0 × L2 with appropriate scalar product, and verify A+I maximal monotone; apply Hille–Yosida. The conservation identity follows by multiplying PDE by ∂u/∂t and integrating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave equation regularity and compatibility conditions (Theorem 10.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u0 and v0 belong to H^k(Ω) for all k and satisfy the compatibility conditions Δ^j u0 = 0 and Δ^j v0 = 0 on ∂Ω for all integers j≥0 (as appropriate), then the solution u is C∞ on Ω × [0,∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization of domains of powers of the wave operator A shows D(A^k) consists of pairs (u,v) with prescribed regularity and boundary vanishing of Δ^j u and Δ^j v up to appropriate orders; apply abstract semigroup regularity theorem (Theorem 7.5) to deduce smoothness.

rubrics_metrics.name: No smoothing for the wave equation; singularity propagation (Remark 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to the heat equation, the wave equation does not smooth initial data: singularities in initial data propagate along characteristics. Example (1D): u(x,t) = 1/2(u0(x+t)+u0(x−t)) + (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} v0(s) ds, so u is no more regular than u0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: one cannot expect instantaneous regularization for hyperbolic equations. Use characteristic analysis to locate propagation of singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-reversibility and group of isometries for wave equation (Remark 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wave equation generates a one-parameter group {U(t)}_{t∈R} of isometries on H (the energy space), i.e., ||U(t)||_H = ||U(0)||_H for all t, and both forward and backward evolutions are well-posed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from A and −A both being maximal monotone and leads to reversible dynamics (change t→−t). Contrasts with the irreversible heat semigroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract variational existence theorem for parabolic problems (J.-L. Lions, Theorem 10.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Hilbert spaces V⊂H⊂V' and a bilinear form a(t;u,v): V×V→R satisfying (i) measurability in t for fixed u,v, (ii) boundedness |a(t;u,v)| ≤ M ||u||_V ||v||_V, (iii) Gårding-type coercivity a(t;v,v) ≥ α||v||_V^2 − C||v||_H^2 with α>0, then for f∈L2(0,T;V') and u0∈H there exists a unique u ∈ L2(0,T;V) ∩ C([0,T];H) with du/dt ∈ L2(0,T;V') solving the variational formulation du/dt(t),v + a(t;u(t),v) = ⟨f(t),v⟩ for a.e. t and all v∈V, u(0)=u0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the parabolic analogue of Lax–Milgram and provides a flexible framework for inhomogeneous/divergence-form parabolic PDEs. Application: choose H=L2(Ω), V=H1_0(Ω), and a(t;u,v) built from coefficients aij, ai, a0 ∈ L∞ with uniform ellipticity (42) to obtain weak solutions of more general parabolic PDEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth coefficients yield C∞ interior regularity (Theorem 10.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is smooth, coefficients aij, ai, a0 are C∞ on Ω×[0,T] and satisfy ellipticity, and f is C∞ while u0 ∈ L2 (or u0∈C∞ with compatibility at boundary), then the solution u belongs to C∞(Ω × [ε, T]) for every ε>0, and under compatibility conditions u ∈ C∞(Ω × [0, T]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof based on parabolic estimates analogous to elliptic ones and the Hille–Yosida/abstract theory. Compatibility at t=0 is required to extend smoothness up to t=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: L2 and Lp regularity results for nonhomogeneous heat equation (Theorems 10.11 and 10.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: L2-regularity: given f ∈ L2(Ω×(0,T)) and u0 ∈ H1_0(Ω), there is a unique solution u with u ∈ C([0,T];H1_0(Ω)) ∩ L2(0,T;H2(Ω)∩H1_0(Ω)) and ∂u/∂t ∈ L2(0,T;L2(Ω)). Lp-regularity: for 1<p<∞ and f ∈ Lp(Ω×(0,T)) (with u0=0 for simplicity) there exists a unique solution with spatial and time derivatives in corresponding Lp spaces (statement continued in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results give quantitative regularity in Lebesgue spaces and are proved by energy methods and functional-analytic techniques. They are the starting point for further Hölder or Schauder estimates when coefficients are smooth.
